article.title: Technical information
article.p: This section contains technical information about using SaxonC:
For technical details about how SaxonC is built see Technical details.

section.title: Limitations
section.p: The following limitations apply to the 12 release:

ul.li: ICU localization is not supported in SaxonC 12.0 to 12.3, but is supported from 12.4.
The XQuery Update feature is not supported.
Host language extension functions are currently not supported.

section.title: Memory management in C++
section.p: This section provides a guide to memory management with the SaxonC C++ API.

The SaxonC C++ API documentation is a good place to start, as this provides information about the input arguments and output from each of the methods. Some API methods return pointers which require manual deallocation of memory. For many of these the responsibility is on the caller. For example, there are a number of API methods which return a pointer to a created XDM object on the heap memory; the caller must deallocate the memory used by calling delete, otherwise memory will be leaked. For instance:

ul.li: The SaxonProcessor parse functions (parseXmlFromString(), parseXmlFromFile(), etc.) return a pointer to the created XdmNode object on the heap memory. The caller must deallocate the memory used by calling delete.
The caller is responsible for deallocating memory for the pointer to the XdmValue object returned by the XPathProcessor methods evaluate() and evaluateSingle().
The caller is responsible for deallocating memory for the pointers to the XdmValue objects returned by various XsltExecutable and XQueryProcessor methods.

section.p: The XdmNode object represents a node in an XDM tree. As a tree is navigated, the child object pointers are created lazily. So when one of the XdmNode methods getChildren(), axisNodes(), getChild() or getAttributeNodes() is called, one or more XdmNode object pointers are created. The caller is responsible for the deallocation of memory using delete. It is important to note that calling these methods from the same node object repeatedly creates the child nodes again; there is no caching.

An XdmItem represents an XDM item (a node, function, or atomic value), and an XdmValue represents an XDM sequence of items. For each XdmValue, the XdmItem objects it contains are cached. Whenever an item is retrieved from an XdmValue using itemAt() or getHead(), the caller is responsible for deallocating the memory for the pointers to the XdmItem objects. Repeated calls access the same objects. (Note that this is different to the case above for child nodes of XdmNode, where these are not cached, and each call recreates the objects.) For example:
Notice in the above example that the pointers item0_1 and item0_2 point to the same object. So it is only necessary to call delete on one of the pointers.

Generally, when retrieving string values using the SaxonC C++ API, a char pointer array is allocated using operator new. This is because the string allocation on the heap is created from the underlying Java code. Callers to these API methods must deallocate the memory used by calling operator delete on the char pointer array.
Note that there are exceptions to this, where the API method creates a string on the stack, and the memory management is internally handled. For instance the SaxonProcessor method version().

section.title: Debugging
section.p: From SaxonC 12.1, exceptions that are thrown from the underlying Java code are handled in the C++ API and re-thrown as a C++ exception called SaxonApiException. Likewise these exceptions are thrown in the Python API as PySaxonApiError, and in the PHP extension as a PHP exception.
If a program crashes, it is sometimes useful to run the program on the command line under the debugger tool gdb for Linux and MacOS, and this may give insight to where the fault occurred.
